title: Sperner’s Lemma
text:
Sperner’s lemma is a combinatorial statement about colorings of triangulated triangles, with two very different classic proofs — one combinatorial, one geometric.














Barycentric Coordinates


Introduces barycentric coordinates on a triangle as the setting for Sperner’s Lemma.












Sperner’s Lemma - Statement


States Sperner’s Lemma on a triangulated triangle and lets you color vertices to test the condition interactively.












Sperner’s Lemma - Combinatorial Proof


Proves Sperner’s Lemma with the ‘doors’ argument: a path that must exit through an odd number of bicolored edges.












Sperner’s Lemma - Geometric Proof


Proves Sperner’s Lemma with a discrete degree argument that counts oriented RGB triangles.

title: Probability
text:
Probability lets us reason precisely about uncertainty: updating a belief in light of new evidence, extracting a signal from noisy measurements, and relating the standard distributions to one another.














Positive Predictive Value


Shows how a test’s positive predictive value depends on disease prevalence, not just its sensitivity and specificity.












1D Recursive Filters


Compares a moving average, an exponential moving average, and a Kalman filter for smoothing a noisy 1D signal.












Distribution Relationships


A clickable map of how the standard probability distributions turn into one another, with each distribution’s density plotted from its own formula.

title: Model Fitting
text:
Model fitting chooses parameters so a model matches observed data as closely as possible. The apps below explore how model complexity trades off against stability: a model with more free parameters can always fit the data at least as well, but it can also become far more sensitive to the data’s noise.














Polynomial Fits


Fits polynomials of increasing degree to noisy data and shows the resulting overfitting.












L1 vs. L2 Regression


Compares least-squares (L2) and least-absolute-deviations (L1) regression on data with outliers.

title: Privacy & Cookies
text:
Visual Math Lab is a static website. Every visualization on it runs entirely in your browser: the functions you type, the parameters you set, and the numbers that come out of them are computed locally and never sent anywhere. There is no backend, no account system, and no database.
The only data that leaves your browser is anonymous usage analytics, and only if you agree to it.

title: Privacy & Cookies
text:
What is collected
If you accept analytics, the site sends a small event to Google Analytics when you open a page, when you scroll to the bottom of one, when you follow a link to another site, and when you leave a page. Each event carries:

the address of the page you are on, and its title
the address of the page that referred you, if any
your screen size and browser language
a randomly generated identifier, described below
how long you spent on the page

Google derives an approximate location (typically city-level) from your IP address. The IP address itself is not stored by Google Analytics 4.

title: Privacy & Cookies
text:
What is not collected

No advertising. Google Signals, ads personalization, and remarketing are all off. Nothing collected here is used to target advertising, and it is not shared with advertisers or data brokers.
No personal information. The site never asks for your name, email address, or any other identifying detail, and has no way to receive one.
No mathematical input. The expressions, parameters, and data points you enter into a visualization stay in your browser. They are part of the page address so that you can share a link to a particular example, but the address recorded in analytics is stripped of that query string before it is sent.

title: Privacy & Cookies
text:
Cookies and local storage
This site sets no cookies. Not for analytics, not for remembering your choice about analytics, not for anything else.
A small number of values are kept in your browser’s local storage instead:

Your answer to the analytics question, so you are not asked again on every page. Stored whether you say yes or no — declining is worth remembering too.
A random identifier, only if you allowed analytics: something like 529229690.1787577926, so that repeat visits from the same browser are counted as one returning visitor rather than several new ones. It is generated on your device, is not derived from anything about you, and is not linked to any other service. A few related values record whether the current visit continues a recent one.
Whether you pinned the navigation sidebar open, regardless of your answer, so it stays as you left it from page to page.
Where you dragged the controls on an interactive chart, regardless of your answer — a legend or slider panel you moved off the curve stays where you put it. One small entry per panel you actually move; nothing is stored for panels you leave alone.

All of it stays on your device. Clearing your browser’s site data for this domain erases every one of these values, and you become an unrecognized first-time visitor who will be asked again.

title: Privacy & Cookies
text:
Changing your mind
Use the Analytics preferences link in the footer of any page. It reopens the same question and shows what is currently set, so you can switch either way at any time. Turning analytics off also deletes the identifier described above.
If you say no, the analytics code is never executed at all — it is not merely told to stay quiet. It is delivered to your browser as inert text, and only becomes a running script if you say yes.
If your browser sends a Global Privacy Control or Do Not Track signal, that is taken as an answer already given: analytics stays off and you are not asked. You can still turn it on deliberately through the footer link.

title: Privacy & Cookies
text:
Why collect anything
To find out which topics people actually read, so that time spent writing new material goes where it is useful, and to notice pages that are being opened and immediately abandoned, which usually means something on them is broken. That is the entire purpose. The data is not sold, shared, or used for any other end.

title: Sperner’s Lemma - Combinatorial Proof
Sperner’s Lemma - Combinatorial Proof
Sperner’s Lemma - Combinatorial Proof
text:
Questions

Design an app for visualizing this proof for any triangulation of a triangle, not just uniform subdivisions. How would you generate random triangulations? How would you efficiently loop through all the triangles?
This proof generalizes to an \(n\)-simplex for any \(n\). For \(n=1\), we recover the case of a line segment. For \(n=2\), we have Sperner’s lemma. What is the statement for \(n=3\)? How would you visualize it?

For \(n=2\), the case of a line segment can be thought of as an intermediate value theorem: if a continuous function \(f\) has \(f(a) < 0\) and \(f(b) > 0\), then there is a point \(c \in (a, b)\) with \(f(c) = 0\). Do you see it? What is the analogous statement for \(n=3\)?

How it works
Mathematics is full of ideas that come alive the moment you can see them move. Visual Math Lab makes them touchable: pick a function, drag a slider, change a starting guess, and watch the idea unfold one step at a time — from root finding and differential equations to probability, model fitting, and combinatorial proofs.
Explore on your own, use a page as a lecture demo, or hand one to students as a lab. Everything here is open source, so it is yours to fork, adapt, and extend.

Sperner’s Lemma - Geometric Proof

Sperner’s Lemma - Geometric Proof
text:
(Signed) Areas
A key observation: if a triangle \(\delta\) is not an RGB triangle, then \(\delta_1\) becomes degenerate — it has zero area. Assume, for simplicity, that the area of the original triangle \((v^R, v^G, v^B)\) is 1. This allows us to use area as a tool to identify RGB triangles.






NoteTheorem: RGB triangles via area



A triangle \(\delta\) is RGB if and only if \(\text{area}(\delta_1) = 1\).


We can rephrase Sperner’s Lemma in terms of area:






NoteConjecture: Sperner’s lemma, restated in terms of area



\[\begin{align*}
\text{area}(\Delta_1) > 0,
\end{align*}\] where \[\begin{align*}
\text{area}(\Delta_t) = \sum_{\delta \in \Delta} \text{area}(\delta_t).
\end{align*}\]


In fact, we will prove the following stronger statement:






NoteConjecture: Signed area at \(t = 1\)



\[\begin{align*}
|\Delta_1| = 1,
\end{align*}\] where \[\begin{align*}
|\Delta_t| = \sum_{\delta \in \Delta} |\delta_t|,
\end{align*}\] and \(|\delta_t|\) denotes the signed area of the triangle \(\delta_t\).


One way to define the signed area of a counterclockwise-oriented triangle \(\delta = (v^1, v^2, v^3)\) is as: \[\begin{align*}
|\delta| = \det \begin{bmatrix} v^2 - v^1 & v^3 - v^1 \end{bmatrix}
\end{align*}\] This is the determinant of a \(2 \times 2\) matrix, and therefore the signed area of \(\delta_t\) is a quadratic function of \(t\).






NoteTheorem: Signed area is quadratic in \(t\)



The signed area \(|\Delta_t|\) is a quadratic function of \(t\).

title: Sperner’s Lemma - Geometric Proof
text:
Sperner’s Condition
At time \(t = 0\), \(\Delta_0\) is a triangulation of \((v^R, v^G, v^B)\), so: \[\begin{align*}
|\Delta_0| = 1.
\end{align*}\]
If the triangulation satisfies Sperner’s condition, then for small values of \(t > 0\), \(\Delta_t\) continues to form a triangulation of the original triangle. This is the only step in the proof where we use Sperner’s condition!






NoteTheorem: The triangulation persists for small \(t\)



If the coloring satisfies Sperner’s condition, then there exists \(\varepsilon > 0\) such that \[\begin{align*}
|\Delta_t| = 1 \quad \text{for all } t \in [0, \varepsilon].
\end{align*}\]


But since \(|\Delta_t|\) is a quadratic function and is constant on an interval, it must be constant everywhere. This gives us the full strength of Sperner’s Lemma:






NoteTheorem: Signed area is constant in \(t\)



If the coloring satisfies Sperner’s condition, then \(|\Delta_t|\) is constant in \(t\). In particular, \[\begin{align*}
|\Delta_1| = |\Delta_0| = 1.
\end{align*}\]


By the theorem above, every non-RGB triangle contributes \(0\) to \(|\Delta_1| = \sum_\delta |\delta_1|\), so only RGB triangles matter. For an RGB triangle \(\delta\), the vertices of \(\delta_1\) are exactly \(v^R, v^G, v^B\) in some order, so \(|\delta_1| = \pm 1\): the sign is \(+1\) if \(\delta\)’s vertices, read in its own (counterclockwise) order, visit the colors in the cyclic order \(R \to G \to B\) — the same cyclic order as \((v^R, v^G, v^B)\) itself — and \(-1\) if they visit them in the reverse cyclic order \(R \to B \to G\). (This is exactly the light-vs-dark hatching in the app above: light ⟋-hatched triangles are the \(+1\)’s, dark ⟍-hatched triangles are the \(-1\)’s.) Summing over all triangles, \[\begin{align*}
|\Delta_1| = |\{\text{counterclockwise `RGB`}\}| - |\{\text{clockwise `RGB`}\}|.
\end{align*}\] Combined with \(|\Delta_1| = 1\) from the theorem above, this gives us the following strengthening:






NoteCorollary: Sperner’s lemma, strong form



If the coloring satisfies Sperner’s condition, then \[\begin{align*}
|\{ \text{counterclockwise oriented RGB triangles} \}|
=
|\{ \text{clockwise oriented RGB triangles} \}| + 1.
\end{align*}\]


Sperner’s condition is crucial in asserting that \(|\Delta_t|\) is constant. If the condition is violated, \(\Delta_t\) is no longer a triangulation of the original triangle — even for small \(t > 0\) — and thus we cannot conclude that \(|\Delta_t|\) remains constant.

title: Sperner’s Lemma - Geometric Proof
text:
Questions
The combinatorial proof of Sperner’s lemma does not require the full Sperner’s condition. All it needs is that the number of boundary RG edges is odd. This condition is guaranteed by Sperner’s condition but is weaker than it. Is there a way to extend the above proofs for this alternate hypothesis?

title: Differential Equations
text:
Numerical methods for ordinary differential equations approximate the solution of an initial value problem \(y' = f(t, y)\), \(y(t_0) = y_0\) by stepping forward in time, using only information already known at or before each step.














Explicit Methods for ODEs


Compares explicit ODE solvers – Euler, midpoint, and RK4 – on the same initial value problem.












Implicit Methods for ODEs


Compares implicit ODE solvers against explicit ones on a stiff initial value problem.












Adaptive Methods for ODEs


Steps an ODE solver with an adaptive step size that shrinks or grows to hold the local error near a tolerance.












Butcher Tableau Explorer


Explores how a Runge-Kutta method’s Butcher tableau determines its stages and order.

title: Piecewise Interpolation
text:
Piecewise interpolation methods approximate a function using simple pieces — straight line segments or low-degree polynomials — fit between a set of sample points. These methods are central to numerical analysis because they let us work with unknown or expensive-to-evaluate functions using only a handful of samples.














Polynomial Interpolation


Compares piecewise linear and natural cubic spline interpolation through a set of points.












Numerical Integration


Compares Riemann sums, the trapezoid rule, and Simpson’s rule for approximating a definite integral.












Adaptive Integration


Refines a numerical integral by subdividing only the sub-intervals where the estimate is still inaccurate.

title: Root Finding
text:
Root finding methods are numerical techniques for solving equations of the form \(f(x)=0\). These methods are central in computational mathematics because many problems cannot be solved exactly with algebra alone.














Bisection Method


Finds a root by repeatedly halving a bracketing interval where the function changes sign.












Fixed Point Iteration


Solves x = g(x) by repeatedly applying g, and shows when that iteration converges or diverges.












Newton’s Method


Finds roots by repeatedly following the tangent line to its x-intercept, converging quadratically near a simple root.












Secant Method


Approximates Newton’s method without a derivative, using the secant line through the last two iterates.
